content:
Toph hated birthdays.

This was not entirely true.

Toph hated other people knowing she had a birthday.

She hated gifts presented ceremonially, surprise parties, singing, speeches, and any situation in which several faces turned toward her at once expecting the correct emotional response.

She liked cake.

This distinction mattered.

“You’re not planning anything,” she said three weeks before the date.

We were eating breakfast.

Aang looked at Katara.

Katara looked at me.

I looked at my tea.

Toph slapped the table.

“You’re all terrible liars.”

“We haven’t lied,” Aang said.

“You haven’t spoken.”

“Exactly.”

“That’s lying with your mouths closed.”

I admired the phrase enough not to argue.

“We won’t surprise you,” Katara said.

Toph narrowed her eyes.

“No crowd.”

“No crowd.”

“No fancy dinner.”

“Fine.”

“No gifts where I have to sit there while everybody watches me open them.”

“Fine.”

Toph pointed toward Aang. “No singing.”

Aang looked wounded.

“Especially you.”

He sighed. “Fine.”

Her shoulders lowered.

“Cake?” I asked.

Toph considered.

“Cake can stay.”

So we planned the least birthday-shaped birthday in history.

Which was how, on the morning itself, Toph woke to find no decorations, no pile of presents, no assembled friends.

Only breakfast.

Aang had made dumplings shaped like badgermoles.

They looked diseased.

Toph bit into one.

“What is this supposed to be?”

“A badgermole.”

“Kill it.”

“You already did.”

Katara gave her a small wrapped parcel.

Toph’s expression changed.

“You said no gifts.”

“You said no gifts where everybody watches you open them.”

Katara stood. “We’re leaving.”

She dragged Aang toward the courtyard.

I followed.

Toph called after us, “This is manipulative!”

“Yes,” Katara said.

We closed the door.

Five minutes later, Toph came outside wearing the new belt Katara had made for her.

Nobody commented.

This was difficult.

Aang vibrated with unsaid enthusiasm.

Toph pointed at him. “Don’t.”

“I didn’t.”

“Your face did.”

The day proceeded normally.

Toph taught classes.

I worked in the academy office because I had promised to leave early.

Katara spent the morning at the clinic.

Aang flew to a council meeting in the next district and returned by lunch.

At midafternoon, a student came running into my office.

“Toph wants you.”

“Is somebody hurt?”

“No.”

“Did a wall get broken?”

The student hesitated.

“Define wall.”

I closed my eyes.

The wall was fine.

Mostly.

Toph stood in the advanced yard with three students around a metal box half sunk into the earth.

“What happened?”

“Nothing.”

“Why am I here?”

Toph kicked the box.

It opened.

Inside were dozens of small metal tokens.

Each had a symbol bent into it.

A wave.

An air spiral.

A square.

A tiny raised fist.

I picked one up.

“What are these?”

Toph crossed her arms.

“Nothing.”

One student behind her made a choking noise.

Toph turned. “Leave.”

They scattered.

I held the token.

The square matched the little filing cabinet she had drawn beside my name on our household agreement.

“These are for us.”

“No.”

“Toph.”

“They’re training scraps.”

“Forty identical training scraps?”

“Repetition is important.”

I smiled.

She heard it.

“Don’t make the face.”

“What face?”

“The feelings face.”

“I’m not—”

“You are.”

I crouched beside the box.

The tokens were not identical after all.

Some carried two symbols. Some three. Some all four. On the reverse of each was a tiny indentation shaped like the academy’s foundation stones.

“What are they for?” I asked.

Toph shifted her weight.

“Emergency markers.”

That sounded plausible enough to be suspicious.

“Explain.”

She sighed.

“If we’re in a crowd and get separated, I can feel one if it hits the ground.”

My chest tightened.

“If somebody’s trapped under rubble, they can tap it against stone. Metal carries vibration differently.”

Practical.

Of course.

“And the symbols?”

“So we know whose is whose.”

“Why are there forty?”

Toph went silent.

I waited.

Finally she muttered, “Because I kept making them wrong.”

I looked at the nearest token.

The symbols were clean.

“Wrong how?”

Toph’s jaw tightened.

“Too thin. Too sharp. Didn’t feel right.”

That was not about engineering.

I reached toward her hand.

Stopped before touching.

Toph put her hand into mine with exaggerated annoyance.

“I wanted something you could carry,” she said.

There.

One of the things Toph would not say until she had disguised it as utility.

“I love it.”

“Obviously. It’s useful.”

“I love you.”

Toph froze.

Her heartbeat jumped hard enough that even I could see the pulse in her throat.

Then she scowled.

“Rude.”

I laughed.

“You don’t have to say it back.”

“I know.”

“I mean it.”

“I know.”

Her hand tightened around mine.

Toph had said love in a hundred ways already.

In training me to move instead of freeze.

In a river stone slipped into my pocket.

In asking before grabbing when my body had learned fear.

In the largest piece of sweet bun pushed onto my plate.

In a metal token made and remade until it felt right beneath her fingers.

Words mattered.

So did not forcing them.

We went home after sunset.

The house was dark.

Toph stopped at the gate.

“You said no surprise.”

“There is no surprise,” I said.

“You’re lying.”

The door opened.

Warm light spilled into the courtyard.

Katara stood inside holding a cake.

Aang stood beside her with both hands clamped over his own mouth.

Toph tilted her head.

“No crowd,” Katara said.

“No decorations,” I added.

“No gifts to open,” Aang said through his fingers.

Toph sniffed.

“Chocolate?”

“Chocolate.”

She walked inside.

We ate cake at the kitchen table.

Nobody sang.

Aang nearly exploded from restraint.

Halfway through the second slice, Toph reached into her pocket and put three metal tokens on the table.

One for Aang.

One for Katara.

One for me.

Aang picked his up carefully.

His eyes shone.

Toph pointed at him.

“If you cry, I’m taking it back.”

“I’m not crying.”

Katara traced the wave on hers.

“These are beautiful.”

“They’re emergency markers.”

“Of course.”

I slipped mine onto the cord around my neck.

Toph heard the small click against the clasp.

Her face changed.

Barely.

Happy.

Later, after cake, after Aang finally sang exactly one note and Toph threw a napkin at him, after Katara fell asleep against the sofa arm, Toph found me in the courtyard.

She leaned against my side.

No preamble.

No joke.

For a minute we listened to the city.

Then she said, very quietly, “You too.”

I looked at her.

Toph’s face was turned away.

“What?”

She punched my arm.

“Don’t ruin it.”

I understood.

I did not ask her to repeat herself.

Some things Toph would not say.

Some things she would say only once, in the dark, with no audience and no demand for the correct expression afterward.

I leaned my head against hers.

“Happy birthday.”

“Don’t push it.”

Toph’s birthday ended with everyone asleep except us.

She sat on the front step with her bare feet against the stone and the ridiculous paper crown Sokka had mailed balanced crookedly on her head.

“You know you can take that off.”

“No idea what you mean.”

“It says Greatest Earthbender Who Is Definitely Not Sentimental.”

“Accurate title.”

I sat beside her.

For a while we listened to the house settle.

Then Toph said, “My parents used to make birthdays into proof.”

I turned toward her.

“Proof I was safe. Proof I was delicate. Proof they were good parents because the cake was expensive and nobody let me walk anywhere without a hand on my arm.”

Her voice stayed dry.

The anger under it was old enough to have roots.

“So you hate birthdays.”

“I hate people deciding what I’m supposed to feel because the decorations are nice.”

“That makes sense.”

“Don’t sound so surprised.”

“I’m surprised you told me.”

She elbowed me.

After a moment, I said, “What would make next year less terrible?”

Toph thought about it.

“No surprise guests.”

“Done.”

“No speeches.”

“Done.”

“Something I can break.”

“Negotiable.”

“And this.”

Her shoulder pressed into mine.

I did not ask what this meant.

I knew better now.

The paper crown rustled in the wind.

When we finally went inside, she left it on the step.

In the morning it was gone.

I found it weeks later flattened carefully inside the drawer where Toph kept important academy papers.

I never mentioned it.

At breakfast the next day, Toph complained that the cake had been too sweet, the singing had been too loud, and Aang’s handmade card had been “an artistic crime.”

She kept the card too.

I knew because she asked me, very casually, where someone might store paper so it would not get bent.

“Purely hypothetical?”

“Obviously.”

I showed her a flat document box.

She kicked my ankle on the way past.

I took that as thanks.

The document box stayed in Toph’s room. So did the paper crown. I learned that respecting her privacy included pretending not to know either fact.

I never told her I knew. She never asked whether I knew. That became another kind of trust.
